title: Low Back Pain (Katishool): Ayurvedic View, Posture, Diet & Care
excerpt: Sitting for long hours, lifting heavy weights, poor posture or ageing — back pain is a complaint in almost every home today. Learn why low back pain happens, how Ayurveda understands it, what sciatica (Gridhrasi) is, correct posture and routine, diet, safe home measures and when you must see a doctor immediately.
content:
“My back is stiff as soon as I get up in the morning and bending hurts” or “the pain runs from my back down to my leg” — people of every age tell us this at the clinic. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), about 619 million people worldwide were affected by low back pain in 2020, and it is the leading cause of disability in the world.

The good news is that most back pain gets better within a few weeks with the right care. Correct posture, staying active and timely treatment matter most. This article is for information only — take any treatment only on the advice of your vaidya or doctor.

What is Low Back Pain?

Low back pain means pain, stiffness or strain in the lower part of the back — from below the ribs down to the hips. By duration it is understood in three ways:

  • Acute — less than 6 weeks; often from a sudden jerk, sprain or lifting something heavy
  • Sub-acute — 6 to 12 weeks
  • Chronic — more than 12 weeks; pain that keeps coming back

In most cases no single serious cause is found — this is called “non-specific” back pain, linked to strain of muscles and joints. In some cases the cause is a slipped disc, a compressed nerve, or wear and weakening of the bones. When the pain travels from the back to the hip, thigh and leg, it is called sciatica.

The Ayurvedic View

In Ayurveda, back pain is called Katishool or Katigraha and is mainly considered a Vata vyadhi (Vata disorder). Pain that travels from the back to the foot is called Gridhrasi, which Acharya Charaka describes beautifully:

स्फिक्पूर्वा कटिपृष्ठोरुजानुजङ्घापदं क्रमात् ।
गृध्रसी स्तम्भरुक्तोदैर्गृह्णाति स्पन्दते मुहुः ॥
— Charaka Samhita, Chikitsa Sthana 28

Meaning: Gridhrasi begins at the buttock and, step by step, seizes the waist, back, thigh, knee, calf and foot with stiffness, pain and pricking, and that part twitches again and again.

According to Ayurveda, ageing, dry and cold food, staying up late, overexertion, injury, long journeys and suppressing natural urges increase Vata, which causes stiffness and pain in the joints, muscles and nerves of the back. In some people Kapha and ama are also involved — then heaviness, morning stiffness and sluggishness are greater. So the aim of treatment is to calm Vata, digest ama and strengthen the muscles and joints of the back.

Main Causes and Risk Factors

  • Sitting for long hours on a chair or hunched over, working on a mobile or laptop with the neck and back bent
  • Lifting heavy weights the wrong way, sudden twisting or a jerk
  • Lack of exercise, weak abdominal and back muscles, obesity
  • Wear of discs and bones with age; weakening of bones in women after menopause
  • Pregnancy, a very soft or sagging mattress, high-heeled shoes
  • Smoking, stress, lack of sleep and chronic constipation

Symptoms and Tests

  • Pain, stiffness or strain in the lower back — worse on sitting, bending or getting up
  • Stiffness on waking in the morning that eases somewhat with movement
  • Pain travelling to the hip, back of the thigh, calf or foot (sciatica)
  • Tingling, numbness or burning in the leg
  • Difficulty straightening the back or turning in bed
  • Heaviness in the legs on standing or walking for long

In most ordinary back pain, an X-ray or MRI is not needed at first; the doctor or vaidya starts treatment after examination and looking at the symptoms. But if there are signs of nerve compression, long-lasting pain or the danger signs listed below, an X-ray, MRI, blood tests, vitamin D or a bone strength (bone density) test may be advised.

Diet: What to Eat, What to Avoid

In back pain, the aim of diet is to keep Vata calm, prevent constipation and nourish bones and muscles. According to Ayurveda, warm, fresh, slightly unctuous (with ghee or oil) and easily digestible food is beneficial.

What to eat

  • Warm, freshly cooked food — daliya, khichdi, moong dal, vegetable soup
  • A little desi ghee or sesame oil in meals (ask your doctor if you have heart disease or high cholesterol)
  • For calcium: milk, curd (in the daytime), paneer, ragi, sesame and green leafy vegetables
  • Vegetables such as fenugreek, drumstick (moringa), bottle gourd, ridge gourd, pointed gourd; spices such as ginger, turmeric, garlic, ajwain
  • Soaked almonds, walnuts, raisins and seasonal fruit
  • Lukewarm water through the day — to prevent constipation

What to avoid

  • Stale, very cold, dry and packaged food
  • Too much refined flour, sugar, fried food and junk food — these increase weight and inflammation
  • Too much tea and coffee, cold drinks, alcohol and smoking
  • Heavy, gas-forming foods such as rajma and chole in large amounts or at night

Correct Posture and Daily Routine

  • Do not take complete bed rest — keep moving gently within the limit of pain; this helps faster recovery
  • Keep your back straight when sitting, with a small cushion behind the lower back; get up and walk a little every 30–45 minutes
  • When lifting, do not bend from the waist — bend your knees, keep the load close to your body and do not twist while lifting
  • Sleep on a medium-firm mattress; if you sleep on your side, keep a pillow between your knees
  • Keep the computer screen at eye level; do not bend the neck and back too much while looking at your mobile
  • Keep your weight under control, walk 30 minutes daily and sleep on time

Yoga and Exercise

Makarasana, Bhujangasana (slowly), Marjari Asana (cat-cow), Setu Bandhasana, single-leg Pawanmuktasana, Tadasana and Shavasana, along with Anulom-Vilom, are considered helpful; gentle exercises that strengthen the abdominal and back muscles are also beneficial. Caution: during severe pain, and in slipped disc or sciatica, avoid forward-bending poses (such as Padahastasana) and jerky exercises; with pregnancy, recent surgery or weak bones do them only after asking your doctor; learn yoga from a trained teacher.

Safe Home Measures

  • Warm compress: 15–20 minutes with a hot-water bag or warm towel — relieves muscle stiffness; protect the skin from burns, especially in diabetes where sensation is reduced
  • Oil massage: gentle massage with warm sesame oil, followed by a warm bath — not if there is injury, swelling or fever
  • Staying active: short walks and gentle stretching through the day
  • Sunlight: 15–20 minutes of morning sun — helpful for vitamin D

Do not keep taking painkillers on your own — long-term use can affect the stomach and kidneys. These measures are only supportive; if there is no improvement in two weeks, get checked.

Ayurvedic Treatment — With Caution

Ayurveda mentions many medicines for Vata disorders and Katishool, such as Rasna, Nirgundi, Shallaki, Ashwagandha, Dashamoola, Eranda (castor), and classical formulations like Yogaraj Guggulu. After examination, when suitable, Snehana-Swedana, Kati Basti and Panchakarma, as well as the clinic’s Agnikarma, Viddhakarma, Marma Chikitsa and Cupping Therapy, may be advised. However:

  • Which medicine or procedure, in what amount and for how long — this is decided by the vaidya only after looking at the cause of pain, stage, test reports, constitution, pulse, age and current medicines.
  • Do not stop medicines prescribed by your doctor on your own — especially blood thinners, diabetes, blood pressure or bone medicines.
  • Some herbs can change the effect of other medicines, so tell your vaidya the list of all your medicines; avoid jerky massage or “bone setting” by unqualified people — it can worsen a nerve or disc injury.
  • During pregnancy and breastfeeding, and for children and the elderly, take any medicine or procedure only on the advice of a vaidya/doctor. Beware of claims like “slipped disc cured from the root” or “guaranteed cure without tests”.

When to See a Doctor Immediately

  • Loss of control over urine or stool, or numbness around the genitals and anus — go to a hospital immediately
  • Increasing weakness in one or both legs, dragging the foot, or being unable to lift the foot upward
  • Back pain after a fall, accident or injury — especially in the elderly or with weak bones
  • Pain with fever, unexplained weight loss, or a past history of cancer
  • Pain that keeps increasing even when resting at night and does not ease in any position
  • Back pain with severe abdominal pain, burning or blood in urine — this may be a kidney or abdominal problem

Summary — Points to Remember

  • Most back pain gets better in a few weeks with the right care — don’t panic
  • No complete bed rest — stay active within the limit of pain
  • Correct posture, lifting the right way and getting up to walk every hour
  • Warm, fresh, Vata-calming food; don’t let constipation build up
  • Medicines, Panchakarma and procedures like Agnikarma only under a qualified vaidya
